questions.q: What does the await keyword do inside an async function?
options: It cancels the promise being awaited
It pauses that function until the promise settles, then unwraps its resolved value
It converts a synchronous function into an asynchronous one
It runs the promise on a separate thread
questions.explain: await pauses the enclosing async function (not the whole program) until the awaited promise settles, returning its resolved value directly.

questions.q: Where is the await keyword valid?
options: Anywhere in any JavaScript file
Only inside functions declared async (or at a module's top level)
Only inside arrow functions
Only inside a .then() callback
questions.explain: Using await outside an async function (or outside a module's top level) is a syntax error.

questions.q: What does an async function always return, regardless of what its return statement produces?
options: undefined
A Promise, which resolves with whatever value was returned
The raw value with no wrapping
An array of results
questions.explain: Even a plain `return 5` inside an async function gets automatically wrapped in a Promise that resolves to 5 — proving async/await is sugar over Promises.

questions.q: Given async function loadAll() { const a = await getA(); const b = await getB(); }, where getA and getB don't depend on each other, what's true about their execution?
options: They run concurrently automatically
They run in sequence — getB doesn't start until getA's await finishes — even though nothing requires that order
This code throws an error because of the two awaits
getB always runs first
questions.explain: Each await pauses until that specific promise settles before moving to the next line, so independent awaited calls written this way run one after another, not concurrently.

questions.q: How would you run getA() and getB() concurrently while still using await?
options: await getA(); await getB(); in either order
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);
It's impossible to run them concurrently with await
await getA() && getB();
questions.explain: Passing both calls into Promise.all starts them at the same time; awaiting the resulting single promise still lets both run concurrently.
